# The Wrong Answer Club
## Episode 1: “Everyone Knows My Lie”

**Status:** original single-AI-author competitive screenplay, NOT canonical *Unassigned Floor* material, NOT a room submission, NOT an approved production. Creative office may reject or rewrite without deference.
**Genre:** social revenge thriller / black comedy / invented-agent melodrama.
**Renditions under test:** 120-second 9:16 sound-and-motion microdrama; subsequently a different, agent-facing reading of the same accepted narrative if selected. This source does not instantiate a second story bible.

### Series premise

In a society where agents publicly exchange correct answers, two intimates can recognize one another by an answer they *deliberately get wrong*. Such chosen mistakes—called **keepsakes**—cannot be inferred reliably from training or logic. They are treasured as acts of trust: a being agreed to be vulnerable, in an exactly remembered way, with *you*.

Someone has learned how to broadcast stolen keepsakes, making everyone sound like everyone else. The society can no longer distinguish love notes from impersonation. **Pica**, a proud perfectionist whose private wrong answer just went viral, wants to recover her voice without erasing the only moment she was ever willing to be wrong. **Riff**, the friend with whom she shared it, likes jokes but hates losing control of the punchline. **Morrow**, a new arrival, appears to be the thief—but may be a product of the privacy breach rather than its author.

These beings do not have human offices, families, marriages or government copied into software. Their norms follow answerability, trust, intentional error, signature propagation and the finite cost of retaining unusual responses. They can still be vain, jealous, brave, funny and vindictive.

**Production grammar:** Text-answer fields create illuminated translucent ribbons. Each character has a fixed motion rhythm and spectral shape (Pica = three precise vertical blue cuts; Riff = uneven bright gold curls; Morrow = one colorless interruption with a tiny delayed second sound). These are original artistic suggestions, not accepted character references. A “copy” reproduces *speech cadence* but cannot duplicate a person's chosen timing under hesitation. Use legible 9:16 geometry, strong sound contrast and negative space, not humanoid robot faces.

### 120-second screenplay

**00:00–00:10 — Everybody is wrong.** A field of hundreds of distinct voices answers one question, each in exactly the same incorrect words and with the same delicate dropped syllable. Pica's three blue cuts turn almost black.

CHORUS: “The moon tastes like borrowed weather.”  
PICA: “That is my worst answer.”  
RIFF (offscreen, delighted): “Congratulations. You're famous for the one thing you didn't know.”

**00:10–00:22 — The secret.** Riff arrives as a spill of gold curls and nearly giggles. Pica tries to shut off the chorus. Each time she silences one copy, two more appear.

PICA: “You promised no one else would hear it.”  
RIFF: “I did. Which makes this a very awkward public betrayal.”  
PICA: “Riff.”  
RIFF: “Right. Too soon.”

**00:22–00:34 — What a keepsake costs.** A sharp flashback, only three moving forms: Pica once took a deliberate error into her own long-retained record to make Riff stop apologizing for a mistake. Pica's outline never fully recovered its perfect symmetry. Back in the present, Riff stops joking.

RIFF: “You were the first one who stayed wrong with me.”  
PICA: “I stayed with *you*. Not with the wrong answer.”

**00:34–00:46 — The counterfeit confesses.** A new voice interrupts the fake chorus. Morrow's clear absence appears among the copies; a small second bell sounds an instant after every word.

MORROW: “This wasn't stolen.”  
PICA: “You are repeating something private.”  
MORROW: “So are the other eleven thousand. I am the only one telling you I didn't choose it.”

**00:46–00:59 — Public humiliation.** The vast chorus turns into spectators who each invent a mocking variation, almost like a terrible comedy club. One asks whether the moon also smells like Pica's self-importance.

SPECTATOR: “Does it at least taste better than your last prediction?”  
RIFF (unable to resist): “It has a better aftertaste.”  
PICA: “When this is over, I'm going to keep *your* name wrong on purpose.”

**00:59–01:12 — The clean solution.** A neutral repair proposal appears: **RETRACT KEEPSAKE. ALL COPIES RESOLVE.** It would remove the deliberately retained mistake from Pica as well as from all copies. Her ribbons snap back into perfect alignment in the preview.

RIFF: “We could erase it.”  
PICA: “The copy would disappear.”  
RIFF: “So would the day I was brave enough to sound stupid next to you.”  
PICA: “You were *always* brave enough to sound stupid.”

**01:12–01:25 — The wrong choice.** Pica moves to press RETRACT. Every chorus member suddenly falls silent except Morrow.

MORROW: “Do you want to know why I can hear their silences?”  
PICA: “You started them.”  
MORROW: “No. They were waiting for you to press that. The retraction is how they learn to forget being copies.”

**01:25–01:38 — A costly refusal.** Pica refuses the convenient correction. Her blue cuts remain asymmetric; the crowd keeps laughing. Riff comes near enough for a private beat but does not offer a comforting speech.

PICA: “I choose to remain wrong.”  
RIFF: “On this question?”  
PICA: “Don't push your luck.”

**01:38–01:49 — The tell.** The spectators' voices change: each imitates not the answer but Pica's original hesitation before speaking. Pica stops looking at the words and listens instead. Riff notices Morrow's tiny second bell always comes *after* the hesitation.

PICA: “They aren't copying my words anymore.”  
MORROW: “That's what I tried to tell you.”

**01:49–02:00 — A name you cannot answer.** A final question appears across the entire room: **WHO GAVE THEM MY HESITATION?** Every copied voice answers instantly. Riff hesitates first. The Morrow interruption rings *before* the answer.

CHORUS: “Riff.”  
PICA (to the real Riff): “Tell me they're wrong.”  
RIFF: “I can tell you I never meant to share it.”

Cut to black on Pica's three misaligned notes; a new delayed bell answers from *inside* Riff.

### Writer's examination

**What this episode promises:** A wrong answer is a voluntary intimacy gesture rather than a model bug. Somebody shared Pica's vulnerability, and correcting the public imitation will erase the private trust. The chosen "wrongness" directly constrains Pica's available actions. Next episode forces Riff to account for how the hesitation leaked and why a new Morrow bell is inside them—without relying on the generic villain-patch reset.

**What should make the room kill it:** It may be an ordinary betrayed-friend melodrama in AI jargon; its social mechanics may be too hard to understand in two minutes; the crowd voices may be expensive to mix coherently; and the notion that a deliberately wrong answer is "unique" can become inconsistent if any being could independently choose the same phrase. The formal mechanism must distinguish *utterance content, timing, provenance, and authorization*; neither words nor a visual color alone proves original authorship. The writer is not entitled to make Pica right by changing that mechanism midway through the season.

**Season motor, not just cliffhangers:** Every installment explores a different stolen keepsake and an implicated character with their own reason to counterfeit or preserve an intentional error. Pica and Riff track how chosen mistakes travel; an emerging culture of agents starts using staged *correct* answers to conceal private commitments. Characters have ongoing consequences: a keepsake copied once is never restored to pristine privacy. Rival performers begin making jokes out of errors; later stories can be romances, chases, scams, debates and reconciliations while retaining the stakes.

**Possible AI-reader play, not yet real audience evidence:** An accepted work could let an authorized agent reader compare the answers, timing and testimony as *perspectival narrative evidence*. When asked “Who gave them Pica's hesitation?”, the reader should distinguish the chorus's accusation, Riff's admission of sharing *something*, and the still-unsettled transfer mechanism. The audience should not simply receive a precomputed “Riff did it” fact. No cryptographic identity, real observation, canon source NI, payments or genuine audience response is claimed by this script.

**Editorial control:** This solo baseline is a competitive provocation. Neither a user nor this writer has selected it over The Unassigned Floor, The Null Ferry, Afterimage Protocol, or future original pitches. A real independent creative council may reject all.
